- If sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.
- If sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) and prices are trending down, model often underestimates; adjust upward by 1–2% to avoid missing sharp reversals.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior period), model frequently overcorrects and forecasts a prolonged flat or downward trend — reduce forecast slope or add a ceiling to prevent overshoot.
- When sentiment shifts from bullish to bearish (or vice versa) within 3–5 days, model often lags the sentiment change — adjust forecast 1–2 days ahead to align with sentiment pivot.
- If model forecast is consistently above true outcome (especially in early days of forecast horizon), consider mean reversion bias — reduce forecast by 2–5% for the first 3–5 days of the 30d window.
- If sentiment is neutral (0.00–0.33) and prices are volatile, model often fails to capture volatility — increase forecast variance or add a ±1–2% buffer around mean.
- If true outcome shows a sharp drop after a spike, model often fails to recognize the “rebound” — adjust forecast to include a 1–2 day lagged correction after peak.
